title: Definition
body_md:
A (real) \emph{Cartan datum} $I = (I,\widehat{A})$ consists of a finite set $I$ and a symmetric  matrix $\widehat{A} \in M_I(\mathbb{R})$ with strictly positive diagonal elements:
\[
\widehat{A} = (\langle i,j\rangle)_{i,j} \in M_I(\mathbb{R}),\qquad 
\langle i,i\rangle > 0,\qquad \forall i \in I.
\]

We then write 
\[
D = \operatorname{\mathrm{diag}}(d_i)_{i\in I},\qquad d_i = \frac{1}{2}\langle i,i\rangle \in (0,\infty),\qquad 
A = (a_{ij})_{i,j\in I},\qquad a_{ij} = 2\frac{\langle i,j\rangle}{\langle i,i\rangle}\in \mathbb{R},
\]
so in particular $\widehat{A} = DA$. We call $A$ the associated \emph{Cartan matrix}, and $d_i$ the \emph{associated multiplicities}. 


We call $I$ \emph{non-degenerate} if $\det(\widehat{A})\neq 0$. 


We call $I$ \emph{of (finite) Lie type} if $\widehat{A}$ is positive-definite and $A \in M_I(\mathbb{Z})$ with $a_{ij}<0$ for all $i\neq j$. In this case, $A$ can be put into blocks which correspond to the irreducible Cartan matrices of types $A$ through $G$.  

We call $I$ \emph{classical} if $I$ is of Lie type, and none of the $E,F,G$-types appear in its block decomposition.

label: DefNilpvN
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{DefNilpvN}
To any word $\mathbf{i}$ we associate the Hilbert space 
\[
\mathcal{H}(\mathbf{i}) = \otimes_{J} L^2(\mathbb{R}).
\]
We consider on $\mathcal{H}(\mathbf{i})$ the positive operators 
\begin{equation}\label{EqXVar}
\mathbf{X}_a = \mathbf{X}_a(\mathbf{i}) = \left(\underset{b<a}{\otimes} \mathbf{k}^{\langle i_a,i_b\rangle}\right) \otimes \mathbf{e} \otimes \left(\underset{b>a}{\otimes}1\right) = \left(\prod_{b<a} \mathbf{k}_b^{\langle i_a,i_b\rangle}\right)\mathbf{e}_a, \qquad a \in J,
\end{equation}
where in the last expression we take the closure of the (strongly commuting) product. We denote the von Neumann algebra generated by the $\mathbf{X}_a$ as 
\[
L_{\hbar}(\mathfrak{n}(\mathbf{i})) = \{\mathbf{X}_a\mid a\in J\}'' \subseteq \mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}(\mathbf{i})). 
\]

We further define the \emph{simple root operators} associated to $\mathbf{i}$ to be the positive operators
\begin{equation}\label{EqGenQUE}
\mathbf{E}_i = \mathbf{E}_i(\mathbf{i}):=  \boxplus_{a \in J_i} \mathbf{X}_a,\qquad i\in I. 
\end{equation}
We denote the von Neumann algebra generated by the $\mathbf{E}_i$ as
\[
L_{\hbar}(N(\mathbf{i})) = \{\mathbf{E}_i\mid i\in I\}'' \subseteq \mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}(\mathbf{i})),
\]
and refer to it as the \emph{quantum nilpotent von Neumann algebra} associated to $\mathbf{i}$.

title: Proof
body_md:
If \eqref{EqPentagonOr} holds, then also 
\[
F_{\hbar}(\mathbf{E})^*s\mathbf{F} F_{\hbar}(\mathbf{E}) = s\mathbf{L} \boxplus s\mathbf{F},\qquad \forall s\in \mathbb{R}_{\geq0}. 
\]
Conjugating with $\mathbf{L}^{it}$ for $t\in \mathbb{R}$, we get 
\[
F_{\hbar}(e^{-2\pi \hbar t}\mathbf{E})^*se^{2\pi \hbar t}\mathbf{F} F_{\hbar}(e^{-2\pi \hbar t}\mathbf{E}) = s\mathbf{L} \boxplus se^{2\pi  \hbar t}\mathbf{F},\qquad \forall s\in \mathbb{R}_{\geq0},
\]
so
\[
F_{\hbar}(t\mathbf{E})^*s\mathbf{F} F_{\hbar}(t\mathbf{E}) = st \mathbf{L} \boxplus s\mathbf{F},\qquad s,t\in \mathbb{R}_{\geq0}. 
\]
Applying the quantum exponential property, we find \eqref{EqPentagon}.

Similarly, we derive \eqref{EqPentagon} from \eqref{EqPentagonOr2}. 

Now conversely assume \eqref{EqPentagon} holds. By functional calculus and the quantum exponential property, we deduce
\[
F_{\hbar}(s F_{\hbar}(\mathbf{E})^*\mathbf{F} F_{\hbar}(\mathbf{E})) = F_{\hbar}(\mathbf{E})^*F_{\hbar}(s\mathbf{F})F_{\hbar}(\mathbf{E}) = F_{\hbar}(s(\mathbf{L} \boxplus \mathbf{F})).
\]
But if $\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B}$ are two positive operators with $F_{\hbar}(s\mathbf{A}) = F_{\hbar}(s\mathbf{B})$ for all $s \geq0$, then $\mathbf{A} = \mathbf{B}$, cf. (the proof of) \cite{DCSSV25}*{Lemma 4.16}. Hence we find \eqref{EqPentagonOr}. The relation \eqref{EqPentagonOr2} is derived in a similar way.

title: Remark
body_md:
From e.g.\ \cite{Wor00}*{Equation (1.37)}, one sees that $F_{\hbar}$ is differentiable at $0$ for $\hbar$ small, with 
\[
F_{\hbar}'(0) = (e^{\pi i \hbar} -e^{-\pi i \hbar})^{-1} = (q^{-1}-q)^{-1}. 
\]
Differentiating \eqref{EqPentagon} at $s=0$ and $t=0$, we find the following infinitesimal equivalent of \eqref{EqPentagon}:  
\[
EF - FE = (q-q^{-1})L.
\]
This is a direct quantization of the usual Heisenberg commutation relation \eqref{EqOrdinHeis} (with $L$ playing the role of a `non-commutative $\hbar$').

label: ExaCompHeis
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ExaCompHeis}
Assume that $\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B},\mathbf{L}$ are positive operators such that $(\mathbf{A},\mathbf{B})$, $(\mathbf{B},\mathbf{L})$ and $(\mathbf{L},\mathbf{A})$ form $\hbar$-commuting pairs. Put
\[
\mathbf{F} = \mathbf{A},\qquad \mathbf{E} = \mathbf{L}\star \mathbf{A}^{-1} \boxplus \mathbf{L} \star \mathbf{B}. 
\]
Then $(\mathbf{E},\mathbf{F})$ form a Heisenberg $\mathbf{L}$-pair at $\hbar$. Indeed, clearly $(\mathbf{L},\mathbf{F})$ and $(\mathbf{E},\mathbf{L})$ are $\hbar$-commuting pairs. We further compute, using the quantum exponential property and the fact that $\mathbf{L}\star\mathbf{B}$ and $\mathbf{F} = \mathbf{A}$  strongly commute,
\begin{eqnarray*}
F_{\hbar}(\mathbf{E})^*\mathbf{F} F_{\hbar}(\mathbf{E}) &=& 
F_{\hbar}(\mathbf{L}\star \mathbf{A}^{-1})^*F_{\hbar}(\mathbf{L}\star \mathbf{B})^*\mathbf{F} F_{\hbar}(\mathbf{L}\star \mathbf{B})F_{\hbar}(\mathbf{L}\star \mathbf{A}^{-1}) \\
&=& F_{\hbar}(\mathbf{L}\star \mathbf{A}^{-1})^*\mathbf{F} F_{\hbar}(\mathbf{L}\star \mathbf{A}^{-1}) \\
&\underset{\eqref{EqFormSumId}}{=}&\mathbf{L} \boxplus \mathbf{F},
\end{eqnarray*}
so \eqref{EqPentagonOr} is satisfied.

Consider the unitary 
\[
U: L^2(Z)\otimes L^2(V) \rightarrow L^2(W),\qquad U(f\otimes g)(v+z) = e^{\pi i \hbar \epsilon(z,v)}f(z)g(v),\qquad z \in Z,v\in V,
\]
where we identify $Z \cong 0 \oplus Z$, resp.\ $V \cong V \oplus 0$. Then an easy computation shows that 
\[
U(\mathbf{q}(z)^{it}\otimes 1)U^* = \mathbf{q}(z)^{it},\qquad U \pi_{\ltimes}(\mathbf{q}(v))^{it}U^* = \mathbf{q}(v)^{it}
\]

Any skew-symmetric space $W$ of the form \eqref{EqSkewDecompTriv} is determined by a triple $((V,\epsilon_V),Z,\epsilon_{Z,V})$, consisting of a skew-symmetric vector space $V$ and a vector space $Z$, together with a bilinear pairing

label: EqIsoCrossWeight
title: Proof
body_md:
We may, without loss of generality, assume that $\mathbf{i}$ is surjective. 

Pick then $i \in I$. We show that there exists a dual simple root vector at $i\in I$. 

Choose $\mathbf{i}'$ and $\Phi$ as in Definition \ref{DefFullExch}. By a similar reasoning as in Section \ref{SecQuantBorel}, we have an isomorphism 
\begin{equation}\label{EqIsoCrossWeight}
\mathfrak{h}'\ltimes L_{\hbar}(\mathfrak{n}(\mathbf{i})) \cong \{\mathbf{X}_a,\mathbf{k}_{\omega}\mid a\in J,\omega \in \mathfrak{h}'\}'':= L_{\hbar}(\widetilde{\mathfrak{b}}(\mathbf{i})) \subseteq \mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}(\mathbf{i})),
\end{equation}
with the $\mathbf{k}_{\omega}$ as in \eqref{EqXVarCart}. A similar statement holds for $\mathfrak{h}'\ltimes L_{\hbar}(\mathfrak{n}(\mathbf{i}'))$. 

Then by equivariance of $\Phi$, we can extend $\Phi$ to a $*$-isomorphism 
\begin{multline*}
\Phi: L_{\hbar}(\widetilde{\mathfrak{b}}(\mathbf{i}))\cong L_{\hbar}(\widetilde{\mathfrak{b}}(\mathbf{i}')),\quad \Phi(L_{\hbar}(\mathfrak{n}(\mathbf{i})) = L_{\hbar}(\mathfrak{n}(\mathbf{i}')),\quad \Phi(\mathbf{k}_{\omega}(\mathbf{i}))= \mathbf{k}_{\omega}(\mathbf{i}'),\quad \Phi(\mathbf{E}_i(\mathbf{i}))= \mathbf{E}_i(\mathbf{i}'),\\ \forall i\in I,\omega \in \mathfrak{h}'. 
\end{multline*}
In fact, we then also obtain an isomorphism 
\[
\widetilde{\Phi} = \Phi\otimes \operatorname{\mathrm{id}}: L_{\hbar}(\widetilde{\mathfrak{b}}(\mathbf{i})) \bar{\otimes}\mathcal{B}((\otimes_I L^2(\mathbb{R}))\rightarrow L_{\hbar}(\widetilde{\mathfrak{b}}(\mathbf{i}')) \bar{\otimes}\mathcal{B}((\otimes_I L^2(\mathbb{R})).
\]
With respect to the inclusion \eqref{EqTensDecompExt}, we clearly have 
\[
\widetilde{\Phi}(L_{\hbar}(\mathfrak{d}(\mathbf{i}))) = L_{\hbar}(\mathfrak{d}(\mathbf{i}')),\qquad \widetilde{\Phi}(L_{\hbar}(\mathfrak{n}(\mathbf{i}))) = L_{\hbar}(\mathfrak{n}(\mathbf{i}')),
\]
\[
\widetilde{\Phi}(\mathbf{K}_i(\mathbf{i})) = \mathbf{K}_i(\mathbf{i}'),\qquad  \widetilde{\Phi} (\mathbf{E}_i(\mathbf{i})) = \mathbf{E}_i(\mathbf{i}'),\qquad \widetilde{\Phi} (\mathbf{L}_i'(\mathbf{i})) = \mathbf{L}_i'(\mathbf{i}').
\]
To prove the proposition, we may hence without loss of generality assume already that $i_1 = i$. 

Now one easily verifies that 
\[
\mathbf{F}_i = \mathbf{L}_i\star \mathbf{X}_1^{-1}
\]
satisfies conditions \eqref{EqCond1},\eqref{EqCond2} and \eqref{EqCond3} of Definition \ref{DefHeisDualOp}. Also condition \eqref{EqCond5} is immediate. Finally, we can write 
\[
\mathbf{E}_i = \mathbf{X}_1 \boxplus \mathbf{Y},\qquad \mathbf{Y} = \boxplus_{a>1,a\in J_i}  \mathbf{X}_a,
\]
and condition \eqref{EqCond4} then holds by Example \ref{ExaCompHeis} applied with 
\[
\mathbf{A}  = \mathbf{F}_i =  \mathbf{X}_1^{-1}\star \mathbf{L}_i,\qquad \mathbf{B} = \mathbf{L}_i^{-1}\star\mathbf{Y}.
\]

which is immediate by the Gaussian commutation relation.


Now by the first commutation relation in Definition \ref{DefHeisDualOp}, we get from \eqref{EqFundamUnit} that
\[
W^*(1\otimes \mathbf{K}_i)W = \left(\prod_{j\in I} e_{\hbar}(\mathbf{H}_j \otimes \mathbf{H}_j')\right)(1\otimes \mathbf{K}_i)\left(\prod_{j\in I} \overline{e}_{\hbar}(\mathbf{H}_j \otimes \mathbf{H}_j')\right),

which by \eqref{EqqCommGauss} indeed reduces to the first identity in \eqref{EqCrodQUE}. Similarly, using those commutation relations and Theorem \ref{TheoHeisPent}, we find 
\[
\operatorname{\mathrm{Ad}}_{F_{d_{i_a}\hbar}(\mathbf{X}_a\otimes \mathbf{F}_{i_a})}(1\otimes \mathbf{E}_i) = \left\{\begin{array}{ll} 1 \otimes \mathbf{E}_i & \textrm{if }i_a\neq i,\\ \mathbf{X}_a \otimes \mathbf{L}_{i} \boxplus 1\otimes \mathbf{E}_i,&\textrm{if }i_a = i,\end{array}\right.
\]
so combined with the second commutation relation in Definition \ref{DefHeisDualOp}, we find
\[
\operatorname{\mathrm{Ad}}_{\prod_{a\in J}^{\longleftarrow} F_{d_{i_a}\hbar}(\mathbf{X}_a\otimes \mathbf{F}_{i_a})}(1\otimes \mathbf{E}_i) = \left(\left(\boxplus_{a\in J_i} \mathbf{X}_a\right) \otimes \mathbf{L}_i\right) \boxplus \left(1\otimes\mathbf{E}_i\right) = \mathbf{E}_i \otimes \mathbf{L}_i \boxplus 1\otimes \mathbf{E}_i

W^*(1\otimes \mathbf{E}_i)W = \operatorname{\mathrm{Ad}}_{\prod_{j\in I} e_{\hbar}(\mathbf{H}_j \otimes \mathbf{H}_j')}(\mathbf{E}_i \otimes \mathbf{L}_i \boxplus 1\otimes \mathbf{E}_i) = \mathbf{E}_i\otimes 1 \boxplus \mathbf{K}_i \otimes \mathbf{E}_i.

title: Proof
body_md:
We prove this by induction on the length $\ell(\mathbf{i})$. If $\ell(\mathbf{i}) = 0$ then $\mathbf{i}$ is the empty word, $\mathfrak{b} = \mathfrak{h}$ and $\mathfrak{b}' = \mathfrak{h}'$. The $\epsilon$-pairing is then just the non-degenerate duality pairing between $\mathfrak{h}$ and $\mathfrak{h}'$. 

    Now assume that $\mathbf{i}'$ is given by concatenating $k \in I$ on the left of the word $\mathbf{i}$. We write $J = J(\mathbf{i}) = \{1,2,\ldots, N\}$, $J' = J(\mathbf{i}') = \{1,\dots,N+1\}$ and $I = \{1,\dots,M\}$, so in particular 
    \[
    (i_1',i_2',\ldots,i_{N+1}') = (k,i_1,i_2,\ldots,i_N).
    \]
    Denote with $\bar{\epsilon}_{\mathbf{i}'}$ the matrix of the pairing between the canonical basis vectors of $\mathfrak{b}(\mathbf{i}') = \mathfrak{h} \oplus \mathfrak{n}(\mathbf{i}')$ and $\mathfrak{b}'(\mathbf{i}') = \mathfrak{n}(\mathbf{i}')\oplus\mathfrak{h}'$, and similarly for $\bar{\epsilon}_{\mathbf{i}}$. The first column in the $\mathfrak{n}(\mathbf{i}')$-part and the $i$-th column in the $\mathfrak{h}'$-part of $2\bar{\epsilon}_{\mathbf{i}'}$ are given by
    \begin{equation*}
       C_1^{\mathfrak{n}} =  \begin{pmatrix}
            \langle 1, k\rangle \\
            \vdots\\
            \langle M, k\rangle \\
            \hline
             0 \\
            \langle i_2', k\rangle \\
            \vdots\\
            \langle i_{N+1}', k\rangle \\
        \end{pmatrix}
        \quad \text{and}\quad
        C_i^{\mathfrak{h}}= \begin{pmatrix}
            \langle 1, \varpi_i^{\vee}\rangle \\
            \vdots\\
            \langle M, \varpi_i^{\vee}\rangle \\
            \hline
            \langle i_1', \varpi_i^{\vee}\rangle \\
            \langle i_2', \varpi_i^{\vee}\rangle \\
            \vdots\\
            \langle i_{N+1}', \varpi_i^{\vee}\rangle \\
        \end{pmatrix},
    \end{equation*}
    respectively. Hence $C_1^{\mathfrak{n}} - \sum_{i=1}^M \langle k,i\rangle C_i^{\mathfrak{h}}$ gives a column consisting of entirely zeros except at the first index of the $\mathfrak{n}(\mathbf{i}')$-part where we get 
    \[
    -\langle i_1', k\rangle = -\langle k,k\rangle = -2d_k.
    \]
Hence $\bar{\epsilon}_{\mathbf{i}'}$ will be non-degenerate if and only if the matrix obtained by removing the first row and column in the $\mathfrak{n}$-part remains non-degenerate. But this gives exactly the matrix for $\bar{\epsilon}_{\mathbf{i}}$, which is non-degenerate by induction.

label: TheoInvWeight

\label{TheoInvWeight}

title: Proof
body_md:
By integrability 
\[
L_{\hbar}(N(\mathbf{i})) = L_{\hbar}(\mathfrak{n}(\mathbf{i})),
\]
and hence also 
\[
L_{\hbar}(B(\mathbf{i})) = \mathbb{R}[I]\ltimes L_{\hbar}(N(\mathbf{i})) = \mathbb{R}[I]\ltimes L_{\hbar}(\mathfrak{n}(\mathbf{i})) = L_{\hbar}(\mathfrak{b}(\mathbf{i})).
\]
We then get from Theorem \ref{TheoModFundMultUni}, Lemma \ref{LemNonDegWord} and Theorem \ref{TheoLeftInvWeight} that $L_{\hbar}(B(\mathbf{i}))$ possesses an nsf weight $\varphi$ satisfying the left invariance condition \eqref{EqLeftInvariance} for all $x\in \mathfrak{m}_{\varphi}^+$. 

Using the properties of $R$ in $\eqref{RefUnitAnti}$, we see that the nsf weight $\psi = \varphi \circ R$ on $L_{\hbar}(\mathfrak{b}(\mathbf{i}))$ satisfies the right invariance condition \eqref{EqRightInvariance} for all $x\in \mathfrak{m}_{\psi}^+$.  

This entails that the strong form of invariance in Definition \ref{DefLCQGFormal} holds, see \cite{KV03}*{Proposition 3.1}.

label: EqIsoTrivAction
title: Proof
body_md:
This follows from the following rank $1$ computation which is well-known, but which we spell out for completeness.

It is sufficient to show that if $i\in I$, there exists an $\mathfrak{h}'$-equivariant isomorphism 
\begin{equation}\label{EqIsoTrivAction}
\Phi: L_{\hbar}(N(i,i)) \cong L_{\hbar}(N(i))\bar{\otimes} L(\mathbb{R}),
\end{equation}
with the trivial action of $\mathfrak{h}'$ on the $L(\mathbb{R})$-component, such that 
\[
\Phi(\mathbf{E}_j(i,i))  = \mathbf{E}_j(i) \otimes 1,\qquad \forall j\in I. 
\]
Now $\mathbf{E}_j(i,i) = 0$ and $\mathbf{E}_j(i) = 0$ for $j \neq i$, while
\[
\mathbf{X}_1(i,i) = \mathbf{e}\otimes 1,\quad \mathbf{X}_2(i,i) = \mathbf{k}^{2d_i} \otimes \mathbf{e},\quad \mathbf{E}_i(i,i) = \mathbf{e} \otimes 1 \boxplus \mathbf{k}^{2d_i} \otimes \mathbf{e},\qquad \mathbf{X}_1(i) = \mathbf{E}_i(i) = \mathbf{e}.
\]
Moreover, if we view the second tensorand in \eqref{EqIsoTrivAction} as being generated by $\mathbf{k}$, then the action of $\mathfrak{h}'$ is implemented on both sides of \eqref{EqIsoTrivAction} by the conjugation with imaginary powers of the operator 
\[
\mathbf{k} \otimes \mathbf{k}. 
\]
Hence using \eqref{EqFormSumId}, we see that
\[
\Phi = \operatorname{\mathrm{Ad}}_W,\qquad W = F_{d_i\hbar}(\mathbf{k}^{2d_i}\star \mathbf{e}^{-1}\otimes \mathbf{e}) \in \mathcal{B}(L^2(\mathbb{R})\otimes L^2(\mathbb{R}))
\]
will satisfy \eqref{EqIsoTrivAction}.

label: EqCrossProdIso
title: Proof
body_md:
We can write $\mathfrak{n}(\mathbf{j}) = \mathfrak{n}(\mathbf{i}) \oplus \mathbb{R} a$, where $a$ refers to the last position of the word $\mathbf{j}$. This decomposition satisfies the hypothesis of Lemma \ref{LemDirSumSkew}, so we can write 
\begin{equation}\label{EqCrossProdIso}
\Phi: L_{\hbar}(\mathfrak{n}(\mathbf{j})) \overset{\cong}{\rightarrow} \mathbb{R} a \ltimes_{\beta} L_{\hbar}(\mathfrak{n}(\mathbf{i})),
\end{equation}
where $\mathbb{R} a \overset{\beta}{\curvearrowright} L_{\hbar}(\mathfrak{n}(\mathbf{i}))$ is determined by 
\[
\beta_{ta}(\mathbf{X}_b) = e^{2\pi \hbar \langle i_b,j\rangle}\mathbf{X}_b,\qquad b\in J(\mathbf{i}),t\in \mathbb{R}.
\]
It follows in particular that $\beta$ restricts to an action on $L_{\hbar}(N(\mathbf{i}))$, giving us the inclusion 
\begin{equation}\label{EqCrossProdInclu}
\mathbb{R} a \ltimes_{\beta} L_{\hbar}(N(\mathbf{i})) \subseteq \mathbb{R} a \ltimes_{\beta} L_{\hbar}(\mathfrak{n}(\mathbf{i})). 
\end{equation}
Now \eqref{EqCrossProdIso} satisfies, for $b<a$, 
\[
\mathbf{X}_b(\mathbf{j}) = \left\{\begin{array}{ll} \Phi(\mathbf{X}_b(\mathbf{i})),& i_b \neq j,\\
\Phi(\mathbf{X}_b(\mathbf{i}))\boxplus \mathbf{X}_a(\mathbf{j}),& i_b =j,\end{array}\right. \qquad \mathbf{E}_i(\mathbf{j}) = \left\{\begin{array}{ll} \Phi(\mathbf{E}_i(\mathbf{i})),& i \neq j,\\
\Phi(\mathbf{E}_i(\mathbf{i}))\boxplus \mathbf{X}_a(\mathbf{j}),& i =j,\end{array}\right. 
\]
while $\Phi(\mathbf{q}(a)) = \mathbf{X}_a(\mathbf{j})$. It follows that  
\[
L_{\hbar}(N(\mathbf{j})) \subseteq \Phi(\mathbb{R} a \ltimes_{\beta} L_{\hbar}(N(\mathbf{i}))) \subseteq \Phi(\mathbb{R} a \ltimes_{\beta} L_{\hbar}(\mathfrak{n}(\mathbf{i}))) =  L_{\hbar}(\mathfrak{n}(\mathbf{j})).
\]
By integrability of $\mathbf{j}$, equality must hold everywhere, so pulling back by $\Phi$ we see that equality holds in \eqref{EqCrossProdInclu}. By the general identity \eqref{EqSliceCrossed}, we can conclude that $L_{\hbar}(N(\mathbf{i})) = L_{\hbar}(\mathfrak{n}(\mathbf{i}))$, i.e.\ $\mathbf{i}$ is integrable.

name: Second Splitting Lemma

label: EqComplPent
title: Proof
body_md:
Write 
\[
\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{C}\star \mathbf{B},
\]
and put
\[
\widetilde{\mathcal{H}} = \mathcal{H}\otimes L^2(\mathbb{R}),\qquad \widetilde{M} = M\bar{\otimes} \mathcal{B}(L^2(\mathbb{R})),\qquad \widetilde{\mathbf{X}} = \mathbf{X}\otimes \mathbf{k},\qquad \widetilde{\mathbf{Y}} = \mathbf{Y}\otimes \mathbf{e},\qquad \widetilde{\mathbf{Z}} = \mathbf{Z} \otimes \mathbf{k}\star \mathbf{e}.
\]
Then we claim that 
 \begin{equation}\label{EqComplPent}
    F_{\hbar}(s\widetilde{\mathbf{Y}}) F_{\hbar}(t\widetilde{\mathbf{X}}) =
    F_{\hbar}(t\widetilde{\mathbf{X}})F_{\hbar}(st\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}})F_{\hbar}(s\widetilde{\mathbf{Y}}),
    \text{ for all } s,t \geq 0.
  \end{equation}
Indeed, writing also 
\[
\widetilde{\mathbf{A}} = \mathbf{A} \otimes \mathbf{k},\qquad \widetilde{\mathbf{B}} = \mathbf{B} \otimes \mathbf{k},\qquad \widetilde{\mathbf{C}} = \mathbf{C} \otimes \mathbf{e},\qquad \widetilde{\mathbf{D}} = \mathbf{D} \otimes \mathbf{e},
\]
note that 
 \begin{align*}
    \widetilde{A} \widetilde{B} &= q^{2}\widetilde{B}\widetilde{A},\qquad && \widetilde{A} \widetilde{C} =  \widetilde{C} \widetilde{A},\qquad && \widetilde{B} \widetilde{C} = q^2\widetilde{C} \widetilde{B} \\
    \widetilde{C} \widetilde{D} &= q^{2}\widetilde{D} \widetilde{C},\qquad && \widetilde{A}\widetilde{D} = \widetilde{D}\widetilde{A},\qquad &&\widetilde{B}\widetilde{D} = \widetilde{D}\widetilde{B}
  \end{align*} 
  and
\[
\widetilde{Z} \widetilde{A} = q^{-1}\widetilde{A}\widetilde{Z},\quad \widetilde{Z} \widetilde{B} = q^{-1}\widetilde{B}\widetilde{Z},\quad \widetilde{Z}\widetilde{C}= q\widetilde{C}\widetilde{Z},\quad \widetilde{Z}\widetilde{D} = q\widetilde{D}\widetilde{Z}. 
\]
Then since 
\[
\widetilde{\mathbf{X}} = \widetilde{\mathbf{A}}\boxplus \widetilde{\mathbf{B}},\qquad \widetilde{\mathbf{Y}} = \widetilde{\mathbf{C}}\boxplus \widetilde{\mathbf{D}},\qquad \widetilde{\mathbf{Z}} = \widetilde{\mathbf{B}}\star\widetilde{\mathbf{C}},
\]
we can compute:
\begin{eqnarray*}
F_{\hbar}(t\widetilde{\mathbf{X}})F_{\hbar}(st\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}})F_{\hbar}(s\widetilde{\mathbf{Y}}) 
&\underset{\eqref{EqQuantExp}}{=}&  F_{\hbar}(t\widetilde{\mathbf{A}})F_{\hbar}(t\widetilde{\mathbf{B}})F_{\hbar}(st\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}})F_{\hbar}(s\widetilde{\mathbf{C}})F_{\hbar}(s\widetilde{\mathbf{D}})\\
&\underset{\eqref{EqPentKash}}{=}& F_{\hbar}(t\widetilde{\mathbf{A}})F_{\hbar}(s\widetilde{\mathbf{C}})F_{\hbar}(t\widetilde{\mathbf{B}})F_{\hbar}(s\widetilde{\mathbf{D}})\\
&=& F_{\hbar}(s\widetilde{\mathbf{C}})F_{\hbar}(s\widetilde{\mathbf{D}})F_{\hbar}(t\widetilde{\mathbf{A}})F_{\hbar}(t\widetilde{\mathbf{B}})\\
&\underset{\eqref{EqQuantExp}}{=}& F_{\hbar}(s\widetilde{\mathbf{Y}})  F_{\hbar}(t\widetilde{\mathbf{X}}),
\end{eqnarray*} 
proving the claim.

Now since $\widetilde{\mathbf{X}},\widetilde{\mathbf{Y}} \,\eta\, \widetilde{M}$, we obtain from \eqref{EqComplPent} that $F_{\hbar}(s\widetilde{\mathbf{Z}}) \in \widetilde{M}$ for all $s>0$, and hence from Lemma \eqref{LemAff} that
\[
\mathbf{Z} \otimes \mathbf{k}\star\mathbf{e} = \widetilde{\mathbf{Z}} \,\eta\, \widetilde{M} = M\bar{\otimes} \mathcal{B}(L^2(\mathbb{R})).
\]
But this necessarily implies that $\mathbf{Z} = \mathbf{C}\star\mathbf{B} \,\eta\, M$, finishing the proof.

label: EqEquatH
title: Proof
body_md:
Write $z = \pi_\mathfrak{b} (\lambda)$. 
    Since $z \in \mathfrak{b} = \mathfrak{h} \oplus \mathfrak{n}$, we have
    \[
    z = H + \sum_{a \in J} t_a a
    \]
    for some $H \in \mathfrak{h}$ and $t_a \in \mathbb{R}$. 
    
    We first show that 
    \begin{equation}\label{EqEquatH}
    H = - \sum_{a \in J} t_a i_a.
    \end{equation}
    As $z = \pi_\mathfrak{b} (\lambda)$ we have $z - \lambda\in (\mathfrak{b}')^\perp \subseteq \mathfrak{d}$. Now for $\omega \in \mathfrak{h}'$ we have
    \[
    0 = \epsilon(z - \lambda, \omega) = \epsilon(z, \omega) = \frac{1}{2}(\langle H, \omega \rangle + \sum_{a \in J} t_a \langle i_a, \omega \rangle),
    \]
    since $\lambda \in \mathfrak{h}'$ and thus $\epsilon(\lambda, \omega)=0$. It follows that
    \[
    \langle H, \omega \rangle = \langle -\sum_{a \in J} t_a i_a, \omega \rangle,\qquad \forall \omega \in \mathfrak{h}',
    \]
    hence \eqref{EqEquatH} holds.

    We now show that the $t_b, b \in J$ satisfy a recursive relationship. Write $\lambda = z + x$ with $x \in (\mathfrak{b}')^\perp$. Then, for $b \in J$,  we have
    \begin{equation}
        \epsilon(z, b) = \epsilon(z + x, b) = \epsilon(\lambda,b) = - \frac{1}{2}\langle \lambda, i_b \rangle.
    \end{equation}
    On the other hand we have
    \begin{align*}
        \epsilon(z , b)
        &= \epsilon(H, b) + \sum_{a \in J} t_a \epsilon(a, b) \\
        &= \frac{1}{2}\left(\langle H, i_b \rangle + \sum_{a > b} t_a \langle i_a, i_b \rangle - \sum_{a < b} t_a \langle i_a, i_b \rangle \right)\\
        &= \frac{1}{2}\left(-\sum_{a \in J} t_a\langle i_a, i_b \rangle + \sum_{a > b} t_a \langle i_a, i_b \rangle - \sum_{a < b} t_a \langle i_a, i_b \rangle \right)\\
        &= - \frac{1}{2}t_b\langle i_b , i_b \rangle- \sum_{a < b} t_a \langle i_a, i_b \rangle.
    \end{align*}
    Combining the two gives 
    \[
    \langle \lambda, i_b \rangle =  t_b \langle i_b, i_b \rangle+  \sum_{a < b} 2 t_a \langle i_a, i_b\rangle.
    \]
    Dividing both sides by $d_{i_b} = \langle i_b, i_b \rangle / 2$ we obtain
    \begin{equation*}
       \langle \lambda, i_b^{\vee}\rangle -2t_b= \sum_{a < b} 2 t_a \langle i_a, i_b^{\vee} \rangle,
    \end{equation*}
    and hence
\begin{equation}\label{EqRecurrenceTb}
    t_b = \langle \frac{1}{2} \lambda - \sum_{a < b} t_a \alpha_{i_a}, i_b^{\vee}\rangle.
    \end{equation}
    Solving this recurrence will finish the proof of the lemma.

    Write $v_0 = \frac{1}{2}\lambda$ and $v_b = \frac{1}{2}\lambda - \sum_{a \leq b} t_a \alpha_{i_a}$ for $b \in J$. Using \eqref{EqRecurrenceTb} we then have
    \[
    v_b = v_{b-1} - t_b \alpha_{i_b} = v_{b-1} - \langle v_{b-1}, i_b^{\vee}\rangle \alpha_{i_b} = r_{i_b} (v_{b-1}).
    \]
    Thus
    \[
    t_b = \langle v_{b-1}, i_b^{\vee}\rangle = \frac{1}{2}\langle r_{i_{b-1}} \circ \dotsb \circ r_{i_1}(\lambda), i_b^{\vee}\rangle = \frac{1}{2}\langle \lambda, r_{i_{1}} \circ \dotsb \circ r_{i_{b-1}}(i_b^{\vee})\rangle = \frac{1}{2}\langle \lambda, \beta_b^{\vee}\rangle.
    \]
    Finally, $v_N = \frac{1}{2}\lambda - \sum_{a \in J} t_a \alpha_{i_a} = \frac{1}{2}\lambda + \alpha_{H}$, but also $v_N = \frac{1}{2}w^{-1}\lambda$, thus 
    \[
    \alpha_{H} = - \frac{1}{2}(\lambda - w^{-1}\lambda).
    \]

2\theta_r - 2\theta_l = H_{\rho} \in \mathfrak{h},\qquad 2\theta_r^{\vee}-2\theta_l^{\vee} = H_{\rho^{\vee}}.

In particular, the element \eqref{EqModElUnref} equals the element \eqref{EqFormModEl}. As the latter element is group-like, and the modular element is also group-like, they must then coincide.

body_md: By the Stone--von Neumann theorem and the explicit formulas for the coproduct, we have that, for fixed $i$, the von Neumann subalgebra $\{\mathbf{K}_i,\mathbf{E}_i\}''$, together with the restriction of the coproduct,   defines a locally compact quantum group, namely the quantum $ax+b$-group (see \cite{Ip13a}*{Section 4}, or \cite{DCSSV25}*{Theorem 5.17} for a complete proof with arbitrary parameter). By \cite{BV05}*{Proposition 10.5}, the unitary antipode and scaling group of $(L_{\hbar}(B),\Delta)$ must restrict to those of the locally compact quantum group $(\{\mathbf{K}_i,\mathbf{E}_i\}'',\Delta)$, which are indeed given by \eqref{EqFormScalGroup} and \eqref{EqUnitAntipodeForm} by \cite{DCSSV25}*{Theorem 6.11 and Theorem 6.12}.

title: Lemma
body_md:
We have
    \begin{equation*}
        \epsilon(\rho, \theta_l) = -\frac{1}{4}\langle \rho,H_{\rho}\rangle,
        \quad \epsilon(\rho^{\vee},\theta_l^{\vee})=-\frac{1}{4}\langle \rho^{\vee}, H_{\rho^{\vee}}\rangle,
        \quad \epsilon(\rho,\theta_l^{\vee})=-\frac{1}{4}\langle \rho,H_{\rho^{\vee}}\rangle,
        \quad\epsilon(\rho^{\vee},\theta_l)=-\frac{1}{4}\langle \rho^{\vee},H_{\rho}\rangle.
    \end{equation*}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We have
    \begin{align*}
        \epsilon(\rho, \theta_l)
        &= \epsilon(\rho, \frac{1}{2}\sum_{a \in J}\langle \rho, \beta_a^{\vee}\rangle a)\\
        &= -\frac{1}{2}\sum_{a \in J}\langle \rho, \beta_a^{\vee}\rangle d_{i_a}/2\\
        &= -\frac{1}{4}\sum_{a \in J}\langle \rho, \beta_a^{\vee}\rangle \langle \varpi_{i_a}, i_a\rangle\\
        &= -\frac{1}{4}\langle \sum_{i \in J} \varpi_i, \sum_{a \in J}\langle \rho, \beta_a^{\vee}\rangle i_a\rangle\\
        &= -\frac{1}{4}\langle \sum_{i \in J} \varpi_i,\rho - w^{-1} \rho\rangle\\
        &= -\frac{1}{4}\langle \rho,\rho - w^{-1} \rho\rangle.
    \end{align*}
    The other cases follow similarly.

title: Remark
body_md:
\label{RemScalingConstant}
The expression (in the exponent) of the scaling constant in \eqref{EqFormScaling} is very similar to the central charge in the setting of $\mathscr{W}$-algebras at a specific level $k$, see e.g.\ \cite{Ar07}*{Page 220}. Although we do not know why this particular value of the central charge relates to the scaling constant in our setting, we briefly mention what is known in general about the connection between $\mathscr{W}$-algebras and quantum groups. Namely, by means of the Feigin-Frenkel duality \cite{FF91}*{Proposition 5}, the generic logarithmic Kazhdan-Lusztig conjecture (see e.g.\ \cite{CDN26} for a discussion and recent progress) gives in the case of the above specific $k$, through the associated screening operators, a correspondence with representation categories of a `modular double' quantum group at dual roots of unity $q$ and $q'$ (see \cite{CL26} for a discussion in rank 1, and references to the literature). The cross term $\langle\rho,\rho^\vee\rangle$ however indicates a particular interaction between the two parts of this modular double, which prevents the complete commutation between the latter. In the Liouville regime, the above connections have also been explored in work of Teschner \cite{Tes11}, see as well \cite{GS19}*{Section 7}. In this setting, the modular dual is implemented through the operators $\mathbf{K}_i^{1/\hbar},\mathbf{E}_i^{1/\hbar}$, which indeed fail to commute strongly with the $\mathbf{K}_j,\mathbf{E}_j$, although they commute (up to a sign) on a dense subspace.

title: Definition
body_md:
If $\mathcal{H}_1,\mathcal{H}_2,\mathcal{H}_3$ are Hilbert spaces, we say that operators $(x,y,z)$ with 
\[
x \in \mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_1\otimes \mathcal{H}_2),\quad y \in \mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_1\otimes \mathcal{H}_3),\qquad z \in \mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_2\otimes \mathcal{H}_3)
\]
form a \emph{pentagon triple} for $(\mathcal{H}_1,\mathcal{H}_2,\mathcal{H}_3)$ if 
\[
x_{12}y_{13}z_{23} = z_{23}x_{12}.
\]
If $x,y,z$ are unitary, we call $(x,y,z)$ a \emph{unitary pentagon triple}.

If $x\in \mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}\otimes \mathcal{H})$, we say that $x$ satisfies the pentagon equation if $(x,x,x)$ is a pentagon triple for $(\mathcal{H},\mathcal{H},\mathcal{H})$.

If $x \in \mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}\otimes \mathcal{H})$ is a unitary satisfying the pentagon equation, we call $x$ a \emph{multiplicative unitary}.

title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{TheoMultUni}
If $\mathbf{i}$ is a fully dualizable word, then the fundamental unitary
\[
W \in L_{\hbar}(\mathfrak{d})\bar{\otimes}L_{\hbar}(\mathfrak{d})
\]
is a multiplicative unitary.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The pentagon identity
\[
W_{12}W_{13}W_{23} = W_{23}W_{12}
\]
can be made sense of as an identity in $L_{\hbar}(\mathfrak{b}) \bar{\otimes}L_{\hbar}(\mathfrak{d}) \bar{\otimes}L_{\hbar}(\mathfrak{b}')$. It is hence sufficient to show that  $(W,W,W)$ is a pentagon triple for $(\mathcal{H}(\mathbf{i}),\mathcal{H},\mathcal{H}(\mathbf{j}))$, with $\mathcal{H}$ any Hilbert space with a faithful normal $L_{\hbar}(\mathfrak{d})$-representation. 

By Lemma \ref{LemPentEqIt} and Lemma \ref{LemBraidPentAlt} (together with an easy pushing through of Cartan elements again), it is by iteration enough to show that $({}^aW,W^{(a,b)},W^b)$ forms a pentagon triple for $(L^2(\mathbb{R}),\mathcal{H},L^2(\mathbb{R}))$, where for $a\in J,b\in J'$ we put
\[
{}^aW = \overline{F}_{d_{i_a}\hbar}(\mathbf{e} \otimes \mathbf{F}_{j_a})\overline{e}_{\hbar}(\mathbf{h}\otimes d_{i_a}\mathbf{H}_{i_a}'),\qquad W^b = \overline{F}_{d_{j_b}\hbar}(\mathbf{E}_{j_b}\otimes \mathbf{f})\overline{e}_{\hbar}(d_{j_b}\mathbf{H}_{j_b}\otimes \mathbf{h})
\]
and as before
\[
W^{(a,b)} =  \overline{F}_{d_{i_a}\hbar}(\delta_{i_a,j_b}\mathbf{e} \otimes \mathbf{f}) \overline{e}_{\hbar}(\langle i_a,j_b\rangle \mathbf{h}\otimes \mathbf{h}').
\]
But once again moving the Cartan part outside (to the right), these pentagon identities split into the pentagon identity for the triple of operators
\[
\overline{e}_{\hbar}(\mathbf{h}\otimes d_{i_a}\mathbf{H}_{i_a}'),\quad \overline{e}_{\hbar}(\langle i_a,j_b\rangle \mathbf{h}\otimes \mathbf{h}'),\quad \overline{e}_{\hbar}(d_{j_b}\mathbf{H}_{j_b}\otimes \mathbf{h}'),
\]
which is easy, and a braided type of pentagon equation for the remaining parts, namely for all $a\in J, b\in J'$:
\[
 \overline{F}_{d_{i_a}\hbar}(\mathbf{e} \otimes\mathbf{F}_{j_a}\otimes 1)\overline{F}_{d_{i_a}\hbar}(\delta_{i_a,j_b} \mathbf{e} \otimes \mathbf{L}_{i_a}\otimes \mathbf{f}) \overline{F}_{d_{j_b}\hbar}(1\otimes \mathbf{E}_{j_b}\otimes \mathbf{f}) 
=  \overline{F}_{d_{j_b}\hbar}(1\otimes \mathbf{E}_{j_b}\otimes \mathbf{f})  \overline{F}_{d_{i_a}\hbar}(\mathbf{e} \otimes \mathbf{F}_{j_a}\otimes 1).\]
But these identities either follow from strong commutation (if $i_a\neq j_b$), or by Theorem \ref{TheoHeisPent} (if $i_a = j_b$).

label: EqWordOpp
title: Example
body_md:
One can see explictly that in type $A_n$, the word 
\[
(1;2,1;3,2,1;\ldots;n,n-1,\ldots,2,1)
\]
is fully dualizable. This follows from the construction of \cite{DCSSV25}, but let us give a direct argument: write in this case 
\[
J = \{ij\mid 1\leq i\leq n, 1\leq j \leq i\},\qquad \mathbf{i}(ij) = j,
\]
with the lexicographic ordering, taking the normal ordering on the $i$-variable and the opposite ordering on the $j$-variable. Then we have 
\[
\mathbf{E}_k = \boxplus_{k\leq i \leq n} \mathbf{X}_{ik},\qquad 1\leq k \leq n.
\]
Let us now write 
\[
\mathbf{Z}_{jj} = \mathbf{X}_{jj},\qquad \mathbf{Z}_{ij} = \mathbf{X}_{ij}\star \mathbf{X}_{i-1,j}^{-1},\qquad 1\leq j \leq n, n \geq i>j, 
\]
so that $\mathbf{E}_k = \boxplus_{k\leq i \leq n} \bigstar_{j=k}^i \mathbf{Z}_{jk}$ for $1\leq k \leq n$. Further write 
\[
Z_{k0} = \mathbf{L}_k \star \bigstar_{i=1}^k \mathbf{Z}_{ki}^{-1},\qquad 1\leq k \leq n,
\]
as affiliated to $L_{\hbar}(\mathfrak{d})$, and put 
\[
\mathbf{Y}_{ij} = \bigstar_{k=0}^{i-1} \mathbf{Z}_{jk},\qquad 1\leq j\leq n, 1 \leq i \leq j. 
\]
Then with 
\begin{equation}\label{EqWordOpp}
J' = \{ij\mid 1\leq j \leq n, 1\leq i \leq j\},\qquad \mathbf{j}(ij) = j
\end{equation}
one verifies that:
\begin{enumerate}
\item The $\{\mathbf{Y}_{ij}\mid ij\in J'\}$, together with the $\mathbf{L}_i$, realize a copy of $L_{\hbar}(\mathfrak{b}'(\mathbf{j}))$, where the word $\mathbf{j}$ in \eqref{EqWordOpp} is determined by giving again $J'$ the total lexicographic order with the opposite order in the second component, so corresponding to the word 
\[
\mathbf{j} = (n,n-1,\ldots,1;n,n-1,\ldots,2;\ldots; n,n-1;n). 
\]
\item The 
\[
\mathbf{F}_i = \boxplus_{j=1}^i \mathbf{Y}_{ji},\qquad 1\leq i \leq n 
\]
form dual simple root operators for $\mathbf{i}$.  
\end{enumerate}
The proof of the first statement is verified by a direct (combinatorial) argument. The second statement is checked by a well-organized iterated application of either strong commutation relations or the pentagon equation (see e.g.\ \cite{DCSSV25}*{Appendix G}). We do not spell out the details here, as it is explained in great detail in \cite{DCSSV25}.

title: Example
body_md:
Consider the Cartan datum of type $C_2$ as in Section \ref{SecCartTypeC}, and consider the words
\[
\mathbf{i} = (1,2,1,2),\qquad \mathbf{j} = (2,1,2,1),
\]
with the quantum torus generators of $L_{\hbar}(\mathfrak{n}(\mathbf{i}))$, resp.\ $L_{\hbar}(\mathfrak{n}(\mathbf{j}))$ written as $\mathbf{X}_1,\ldots,\mathbf{X}_4$, resp.\ $\mathbf{Z}_1,\ldots,\mathbf{Z}_4$. Put 
\[
U = F_{\hbar}(\mathbf{X}_2\star \mathbf{X}_4^{-1})F_{2\hbar}(\mathbf{X}_1\star \mathbf{X}_3^{-1})F_{\hbar}(\mathbf{X}_2^{-1}\star \mathbf{X}_4),
\]
and put 
\[
\mathbf{X}_1' = \mathbf{X}_4,\qquad \mathbf{X}_2' = \mathbf{X}_2^2\star \mathbf{X}_3\star \mathbf{X}_4^{-2},\qquad \mathbf{X}_3' = \mathbf{X}_2^{-1}\star \mathbf{X}_4^2,\qquad \mathbf{X}_4' = \mathbf{X}_1\star \mathbf{X}_2^2 \star \mathbf{X}_4^{-2}.
\]
Then it follows from the results in Section \ref{Secmij4} that we can identify $L_{\hbar}(\mathfrak{b}(\mathbf{j})) \cong L_{\hbar}(\mathfrak{b}(\mathbf{i}))$ in such a way that 
\[
\mathbf{Z}_i = U \mathbf{X}_i' U^*,\qquad \mathbf{E}_1 = \mathbf{X}_1\boxplus \mathbf{X}_3 = \mathbf{Z}_2\boxplus \mathbf{Z}_4,\qquad \mathbf{E}_2 = \mathbf{X}_2\boxplus \mathbf{X}_4 = \mathbf{Z}_1 \boxplus \mathbf{Z}_3.  
\]
From the proof of Proposition \ref{PropExchDual}, we then know that 
\[
\mathbf{F}_1 = \mathbf{X}_1^{-1}\star \mathbf{L}_1,\qquad \mathbf{F}_2 = \mathbf{Z}_1^{-1}\star \mathbf{L}_2
\]
will be dual simple root operators for $\mathbf{i}$, affiliated to $L_{\hbar}(\mathfrak{d}(\mathbf{i}))$. To show that $\mathbf{i}$ is fully dualizable, we hence need to realize $\mathbf{F}_1$ and $\mathbf{F}_2$ in Feigin form. 

For this, put 
\[
V = F_{\hbar}(\mathbf{X}_2\star \mathbf{X}_4^{-1})F_{2\hbar}(\mathbf{X}_1\star \mathbf{X}_3^{-1}). 
\]
Then one computes from \eqref{EqFormSumIdAlt} that 
\[
\mathbf{Z}_1^{-1}= U \mathbf{X}_4^{-1} U^* = V (\mathbf{X}_4^{-1}\boxplus \mathbf{X}_2^{-1})V^*,
\]
\[
V^* \mathbf{X}_1^{-1}V = F_{2\hbar}(\mathbf{X}_1\star \mathbf{X}_3^{-1})^* \mathbf{X}_1^{-1} F_{2\hbar}(\mathbf{X}_1\star \mathbf{X}_3^{-1}) = \mathbf{X}_1^{-1}\boxplus \mathbf{X}_3^{-1},
\]
so 
\[
V^* \mathbf{F}_1 V = \mathbf{Y}_1 \boxplus \mathbf{Y}_3,\qquad V^* \mathbf{F}_2V = \mathbf{Y}_2\boxplus \mathbf{Y}_4,\qquad  V^*\mathbf{L}_1V = \mathbf{L}_1,\qquad V^*\mathbf{L}_2V = \mathbf{L}_2,
\]
with 
\[
\mathbf{Y}_1 = \mathbf{L}_1\star \mathbf{X}_1^{-1},\qquad \mathbf{Y}_2 = \mathbf{L}_2\star \mathbf{X}_2^{-1},\qquad \mathbf{Y}_3 = \mathbf{L}_1\star \mathbf{X}_3^{-1},\qquad \mathbf{Y}_4 = \mathbf{L}_2\star \mathbf{X}_4^{-1}. 
\]
It is now easily checked that the $\mathbf{Y}_a$ and $\mathbf{L}_i$ provide a Feigin realization of $L_{\hbar}(\mathfrak{b}'(\mathbf{i}))$, with $\mathbf{i}$ the word $(1,2,1,2)$ as before.
